schools.summary: Ellicott reads the opening and as the illative conjunction common to all the historical books, marking the unity of the history without implying continuity of time or authorship with Samuel, and notes that the clothes are bed-clothes, so that the king could no longer rise; he traces so complete a decrepitude at no great age to a life that took up its responsibilities early, was hard and trying throughout, and not wholly free from self-indulgence. Keil and Delitzsch place Shunem at the modern Sulem or Solam and explain the closing remark that the king knew her not as recorded neither to show David impotent nor to deny that she became his concubine, but only to account for Adonijah's later suit for her, the whole affair being judged by the standards of a time when polygamy gave no offence.

Henry reads the decrepitude as chastisement, David being punished for his former sins and especially the matter of Uriah, and feeling the hardships of a youth he then made nothing of, from which he draws the warning that the strong man should not glory in his strength and the young should remember their Creator before the evil days come. He judges the physicians weak and unskilful, knowing no relief but outward applications, and their second prescription foolish in a man who should rather have been preparing for his funeral, holding that David's prophets should have been consulted along with his physicians; Abishag he takes for a secondary wife, married before he lay with her.

Clarke puts David at about sixty-nine, dying in his seventieth year, and dates the chapter about a year before his death, attributing the premature decay to fatigues and family afflictions and to wasting maladies the Psalms often mention. He defends the second prescription on medical grounds as the best the case admitted, the exhausted frame drawing animal heat from a young and healthy body, identifies it with Friar Bacon's secret for the cure of old age, and reads the king knew her not by the same physician's maxim, that one takes all one can from the medicine and gives nothing back.

Gill fixes the age at exactly seventy, since David was thirty at his accession and reigned forty years, just the age of man, identifies the servants who give the advice as his physicians, and notes that a fair damsel was sought so that she might be acceptable to the king rather than endured in his sight.

debates: How old David was at this point: Gill makes it exactly seventy, Clarke about sixty-nine with these events falling a year before his death, Ellicott simply about seventy
Whether the second prescription was sound medicine or folly: Clarke defends it as the best the case admitted and Henry calls the physicians unskilful and the advice itself foolish

Why it is recorded that the king knew her not: Keil and Delitzsch to account for Adonijah's later suit, Clarke as a physician's maxim about giving nothing to the medicine, Henry as showing her a secondary wife
outliers: Ellicott reports the conjecture that Abishag is the fair Shulamite of the Song of Solomon, and thinks it throws light on the following chapter
Ellicott holds that the opening conjunction implies nothing of continuity of time or authorship with the books of Samuel, the narrative being hardly continuous with them
Keil and Delitzsch and Ellicott agree that the whole notice of Abishag is introduced only for the sake of her later connection with the fate of Adonijah
themes: the winter of a great life
a remedy that gratified the physicians
chastisement felt in the body
a notice introduced for the sake of what follows
1.pericope_label: Now king David was old and stricken in years; and they covered him with clothes, but he gat no heat. Wherefore his servants said unto him, Let there be sought for my lord the king a young virgin: and let her stand before the king, and let her cherish him, and let her lie in thy bosom, that my lord the king may get heat. So they sought for a fair damsel throughout all the coasts of Israel, and found Abishag a Shunammite, and brought her to the king. And the damsel was very fair, and cherished the king, and ministered to him: but the king knew her not.

schools.summary: Ellicott makes Adonijah David's fourth son, born in Hebron at least thirty-three years before, claiming the throne as now the eldest since Chileab had died with Amnon and Absalom, and lists the resemblances to Absalom the narrative itself suggests, personal beauty, favour with a too-indulgent father, ambition and trust in popularity, with the fifty runners, the chariots and horsemen and the festal sacrifice all exactly imitated from that model; but he denies him the craft and ruthless determination of the elder rebel and calls the attempt crude, ill-planned and wanting in promptitude. Keil and Delitzsch reach the same claim by birth order, Adonijah being born after Absalom, call the father's want of discipline a weak oversight that encouraged the attempt, give Joab the motive of a quarrel with David and hope of influence under a new king, and confess they cannot say what moved Abiathar unless jealousy of Zadok.

Henry does the chapter's closest reading of the father's fault, observing that the text does not say the son never displeased his father but that the father never displeased the son, by crossing his humours, denying him anything, calling him to account, keeping him to his business or reproving what he saw amiss, so that the fault was double, the son's in taking reproof for an affront and the father's in withholding it; those who honour their sons more than God forfeit the honour they might have expected from them. On Joab and Abiathar he refuses a motive altogether and finds the thing a wonder, concluding that God left them to themselves, perhaps to correct them for some former misconduct with a scourge of their own making.

Clarke says only that Adonijah was evidently the eldest son then living and particularly loved by his father, and that in the chariots and horsemen he copied his brother Absalom in every respect. On the feast he holds that with Abiathar present the animals were undoubtedly offered sacrificially and the guests fed on the victims, so that the usurper gave a popular colour to his pretensions by affecting to receive his authority from God.

Gill explains the ambition from the father's infirmity and the son's standing as eldest and comely, charges David with the sin of Eli in never correcting him, and accounts for the choice of Joab and Abiathar by their offices, the one commanding the soldiery and the other being high priest with a share in the affections of the people and the office of anointing a king, adding that Adonijah applied to them knowing them to be on some accounts discontented. The meal he treats as a banquet only, large and elegant for a numerous party, without mention of sacrifice.

debates: Whether the meal at En-rogel was a sacrifice or a banquet: Clarke and Keil and Delitzsch make it a solemn sacrificial meal at which he was proclaimed, Gill a feast only, while Henry reports the sacrificial reading as the opinion of some

Why Joab and Abiathar joined the attempt: Gill from their offices and a standing discontent, Keil and Delitzsch from Joab's quarrel with David and a guess at Abiathar's jealousy of Zadok, Henry from no motive at all but a judicial abandonment by God

On what ground Adonijah claimed the crown: Clarke that he was simply the eldest then living, Ellicott that he claimed as eldest since Chileab was dead, Keil and Delitzsch that being born after Absalom he seemed nearest once Absalom was gone
outliers: Ellicott refuses to let the Absalom parallel flatter Adonijah, finding his attempt crude and ill-planned in conception and wanting in promptitude of action
Gill charges David with the sin of Eli in the matter of indulgence, and says Adonijah presumed upon it
Henry holds that a man who has given proof of resolute adherence to what is good will not even be asked to join a bad design, which is why Zadok, Benaiah and Nathan were never approached
themes: a father who never crossed his son
an usurpation modelled on an older one
a feast that served as a coronation
old servants lost to a bad cause
5.pericope_label: Then Adonijah the son of Haggith exalted himself, saying, I will be king: and he prepared him chariots and horsemen, and fifty men to run before him. And his father had not displeased him at any time in saying, Why hast thou done so? and he also was a very goodly man; and his mother bare him after Absalom. And he conferred with Joab the son of Zeruiah, and with Abiathar the priest: and they following Adonijah helped him. But Zadok the priest, and Benaiah the son of Jehoiada, and Nathan the prophet, and Shimei, and Rei, and the mighty men which belonged to David, were not with Adonijah. And Adonijah slew sheep and oxen and fat cattle by the stone of Zoheleth, which is by En–rogel, and called all his brethren the king’s sons, and all the men of Judah the king’s servants: But Nathan the prophet, and Benaiah, and the mighty men, and Solomon his brother, he called not.

schools.summary: Ellicott finds Nathan's initiative natural, since he had been the medium both of the promise of a son who should build the house and of the blessing embodied in the name Jedidiah, and suggests the conspirators held aloof from him for that very reason; he judges that the usurpation would of course be sealed with Solomon's blood but that Bathsheba need hardly have been sacrificed, except that her favour would excite jealousy and Solomon, being young, might be thought her instrument, he grounds David's right to name a successor in Oriental custom, and he marks a growth of court ceremony since Absalom's defeat which makes entering the bedchamber an intrusion. Keil and Delitzsch hold that had Adonijah secured the throne he would have put both Solomon and his mother out of the way by the barbarous custom of the East, as political opponents.

Henry observes who did not know, that David knew nothing because disobedient children think themselves well off if they can keep a good old parent ignorant, that Bathsheba lived retired and knew nothing either, and that Solomon probably knew and was as a deaf man that heard not, leaving the matter to God and his friends. He grounds the appeal to David in prophecy rather than prerogative, denying that any prince may bequeath his subjects by will as goods and chattels and holding that Israel waited on David as a prophet by whom the Spirit of the Lord spoke, and he reads Bathsheba's address as discreet in four steps, the oath, the news, the pointed omission of Solomon from the invitation, and the danger.

Clarke takes Adonijah to have been considered legally appointed and about to exercise the office, assumes that both Bathsheba and Solomon would have been put to death as state criminals, and breaks out against the cursed lust of rule by which a father will destroy his son, a son depose his father and a brother murder a brother. He thinks the oath very likely made and known only to Bathsheba and Nathan, states that the monarchy was neither hereditary nor elective since the king simply named his successor, and adds an excursus of his own preferring hereditary monarchy to elective as safer for the state and more secure for the subject.

debates: Whose life stood in danger: Keil and Delitzsch and Clarke hold that Adonijah would have killed both Solomon and his mother, while Ellicott judges that Bathsheba need hardly have been sacrificed and explains her danger from jealousy of her favour

Where the oath came from, since it is recorded nowhere else: Clarke thinks it genuine and known only to Bathsheba and Nathan, Ellicott assigns it to the time of Solomon's birth and points to an apparently earlier designation in Chronicles

On what footing Israel waited for David's word: Clarke that the king simply named his successor in a monarchy neither hereditary nor elective, Ellicott that the prerogative belonged to the reigning king by Oriental custom, Henry that David was heard not as a king but as a prophet
outliers: Clarke leaves the narrative to argue that hereditary monarchy carries a high balance of evidence over the elective and is every way safer for the state and more secure for the subject

Ellicott reads a growth of royal state and Oriental reverence since the defeat of Absalom, preparatory to the greater majesty of Solomon, so that Bathsheba's entry into the bedchamber is an intrusion ventured only as a suppliant
Henry denies that it is any prerogative of a prince to bequeath his subjects by will, as though they were his goods and chattels
themes: a king who knew nothing of it
an oath recorded nowhere else
a succession that waited on prophecy
the growth of a court
11.pericope_label: Wherefore Nathan spake unto Bath–sheba the mother of Solomon, saying, Hast thou not heard that Adonijah the son of Haggith doth reign, and David our lord knoweth it not? Now therefore come, let me, I pray thee, give thee counsel, that thou mayest save thine own life, and the life of thy son Solomon. Go and get thee in unto king David, and say unto him, Didst not thou, my lord, O king, swear unto thine handmaid, saying, Assuredly Solomon thy son shall reign after me, and he shall sit upon my throne? why then doth Adonijah reign? Behold, while thou yet talkest there with the king, I also will come in after thee, and confirm thy words. And Bath–sheba went in unto the king into the chamber: and the king was very old; and Abishag the Shunammite ministered unto the king. And Bath–sheba bowed, and did obeisance unto the king. And the king said, What wouldest thou? And she said unto him, My lord, thou swarest by the Lord thy God unto thine handmaid, saying, Assuredly Solomon thy son shall reign after me, and he shall sit upon my throne. And now, behold, Adonijah reigneth; and now, my lord the king, thou knowest it not: And he hath slain oxen and fat cattle and sheep in abundance, and hath called all the sons of the king, and Abiathar the priest, and Joab the captain of the host: but Solomon thy servant hath he not called. And thou, my lord, O king, the eyes of all Israel are upon thee, that thou shouldest tell them who shall sit on the throne of my lord the king after him. Otherwise it shall come to pass, when my lord the king shall sleep with his fathers, that I and my son Solomon shall be counted offenders.

schools.summary: Ellicott takes Nathan's question whether David had said that Adonijah should reign as merely drawing out a denial, and finds it true to nature that it does so by assuming, as court language would, that nothing of the kind could be conceived as done without the king's will; he marks the contrast between Nathan so deferential on business of state and the bold superiority of his tone in his true prophetic office, and calls the adjuration about the soul redeemed out of all distress characteristic of David but peculiarly appropriate in an old man near the haven of rest. Keil and Delitzsch report Bathsheba's withdrawal with the deepest prostration and a blessing out of her inmost gratitude, and note that the formula may the king live for ever was used by Israelites only on occasions of special importance while Babylonians and Persians used it constantly.

Henry makes the timing the point, that Nathan seconded Bathsheba before the king could answer lest he should be dilatory and say he would consider of it, whereas out of the mouth of two such witnesses the word would be established; he observes that Nathan paid the same reverence to a king sick in bed as on his throne yet dealt more plainly than Bathsheba had, and turns the prophet's question into a dilemma of three limbs. On the oath he dwells, that an oath is so sacred its obligation cannot be broken and so solemn its impression cannot be forgotten, and that dying saints ought to be witnesses for God and speak of him as they have found him.

Clarke alone attends to the procedure, noting that Bathsheba had gone out when Nathan came in and withdrew when she was called back, so that each had a separate audience, and that to Nathan the king expressed no will at all.

Gill notices the pretence kept up, Nathan telling his story as though he knew nothing of Bathsheba's application and the king had never heard of the matter, marks the geography of the report that Adonijah had gone down from Jerusalem which lay high to the stone of Zoheleth in the valley, and observes that to his former oath David added another for greater confirmation.

debates: What Nathan's question is doing: Ellicott takes it as merely drawing out a denial in the natural idiom of a court, Henry makes it a dilemma of three limbs designed to force David to clear himself

What weight the closing blessing carries: Keil and Delitzsch make may the king live for ever a formula reserved by Israelites for occasions of special importance, Ellicott flattens it to the same acclamation given to Adonijah at the feast, Henry takes it at full weight as a prayer that David might live for ever if it were possible
outliers: Clarke observes that each petitioner had a separate audience and that to Nathan the king expressed no will at all
Ellicott contrasts Nathan's deference as a counsellor on state business with the bold superiority of his tone when discharging his true prophetic office
Henry holds that good men would do their duty if they were reminded of it, and that those who act as their remembrancers do them a real kindness
themes: two witnesses before a failing king
an oath renewed with another
reverence paid to a sick bed
a soul redeemed out of all distress
22.pericope_label: And, lo, while she yet talked with the king, Nathan the prophet also came in. And they told the king, saying, Behold Nathan the prophet. And when he was come in before the king, he bowed himself before the king with his face to the ground. And Nathan said, My lord, O king, hast thou said, Adonijah shall reign after me, and he shall sit upon my throne? For he is gone down this day, and hath slain oxen and fat cattle and sheep in abundance, and hath called all the king’s sons, and the captains of the host, and Abiathar the priest; and, behold, they eat and drink before him, and say, God save king Adonijah. But me, even me thy servant, and Zadok the priest, and Benaiah the son of Jehoiada, and thy servant Solomon, hath he not called. Is this thing done by my lord the king, and thou hast not shewed it unto thy servant, who should sit on the throne of my lord the king after him? Then king David answered and said, Call me Bath–sheba. And she came into the king’s presence, and stood before the king. And the king sware, and said, As the Lord liveth, that hath redeemed my soul out of all distress, Even as I sware unto thee by the Lord God of Israel, saying, Assuredly Solomon thy son shall reign after me, and he shall sit upon my throne in my stead; even so will I certainly do this day. Then Bath–sheba bowed with her face to the earth, and did reverence to the king, and said, Let my lord king David live for ever.

schools.summary: Ellicott opens on the change in David, the sudden flash of the old energy and the terse directions for every part of the inauguration striking against the despondency with which, far younger, he had taken the news of Absalom's rebellion, since then he felt a threatened chastisement coming and now knows it past; he notices the completeness of the provision, the royal mule and body-guard marking the royal sanction, the anointing the sanction of priest and prophet, the acclamation the adhesion of the people, with enthronement and homage to follow, doubts whether Gihon lay west or south of the city, and reads the shouting as more than conventional loyalty. Keil and Delitzsch explain the mule as a sign of succession, compare the Persian honour of riding the king's horse, and report the unanimous opinion of the Rabbins that where a succession was unquestioned there was no anointing at all.

Henry reasons from Solomon's position that the unction was what settled a contested title, he being no first of his line as Saul and David were but a younger son made king by divine appointment, and turns the point against the usurper in a sentence, that we do not find Abiathar pretending to anoint Adonijah, who was made king by a feast and not by an unction, and that whom God calls he will qualify. He holds that the wisest and best man desires his children to be wiser and better than himself, and that the power of a prince can be little satisfaction to him unless he knows it satisfies his people.

Clarke puts the mule as law rather than sign, since no subject could use anything belonging to the prince without forfeiting his life, so that the offer was full evidence of the appointment, and sets out the inauguration in four steps, adding that the king elect was taken to a public well or river where the concourse was greatest so that all might see who was appointed and that the continual stream at Gihon denoted the perpetuity of the kingdom. On Benaiah's prayer he observes drily that a wish that a son should surpass his father is borne from a son but is no compliment in ordinary cases, and quotes a Latin panegyrist whose words to an emperor run close to Benaiah's.

Gill draws from the servants of your lord the rabbinic inference that a king stands above a high priest, since David here calls himself lord of Zadok the priest and Nathan the prophet, and holds that the oil came from the tent David had pitched for the ark rather than the tabernacle at Gibeon, which was too far off when haste was required, reporting but disapproving Kimchi's view that it stood at Gibeon and was fetched thence.

debates: Where the anointing oil came from: Gill, Keil and Delitzsch and Ellicott all place it in the tent on Zion rather than the tabernacle at Gibeon, Gill reporting and rejecting Kimchi's contrary view and Ellicott noting the awkwardness that haste forced the nearer source though Abiathar presided there and Zadok only at Gibeon

Why an anointing was needed at all: Keil and Delitzsch from the Rabbins, that an unquestioned succession required none and this title had been made doubtful while the old king lived, Henry from Solomon's standing as a younger son made king by divine appointment against a contested claim

Whether Benaiah's wish for a greater throne was flattery: Keil and Delitzsch defend him as having the prosperity of the monarchy in view, Clarke observes that such a wish is tolerable only from a son, Henry that the best men desire their children better than themselves
outliers: Ellicott contrasts this flash of decisive energy with David's timidity at the news of Absalom's rebellion, and explains it by his knowing the threatened chastisement now past
Gill reports the rabbinic inference that a king is superior to a high priest, drawn from David calling himself lord of Zadok and Nathan
Henry observes that Adonijah was made king by a feast and not by an unction, and that usurpers had no anointing
Ellicott concludes from the popular acclamation that Adonijah had the great men and perhaps the army but no popular following at all
themes: the old energy returning
a mule that named an heir
sanctions royal, priestly and popular
a kingdom proclaimed at a running stream
32.pericope_label: And king David said, Call me Zadok the priest, and Nathan the prophet, and Benaiah the son of Jehoiada. And they came before the king. The king also said unto them, Take with you the servants of your lord, and cause Solomon my son to ride upon mine own mule, and bring him down to Gihon: And let Zadok the priest and Nathan the prophet anoint him there king over Israel: and blow ye with the trumpet, and say, God save king Solomon. Then ye shall come up after him, that he may come and sit upon my throne; for he shall be king in my stead: and I have appointed him to be ruler over Israel and over Judah. And Benaiah the son of Jehoiada answered the king, and said, Amen: the Lord God of my lord the king say so too. As the Lord hath been with my lord the king, even so be he with Solomon, and make his throne greater than the throne of my lord king David. So Zadok the priest, and Nathan the prophet, and Benaiah the son of Jehoiada, and the Cherethites, and the Pelethites, went down, and caused Solomon to ride upon king David’s mule, and brought him to Gihon. And Zadok the priest took an horn of oil out of the tabernacle, and anointed Solomon. And they blew the trumpet; and all the people said, God save king Solomon. And all the people came up after him, and the people piped with pipes, and rejoiced with great joy, so that the earth rent with the sound of them.

schools.summary: Ellicott calls it one of the narrative's life-like touches that amid the revelry it is the old warrior Joab who catches the trumpet while Adonijah affects to disregard it, finds nothing more striking than so humiliating a collapse in a plot supported by Joab and Abiathar when set against Absalom's formidable rebellion, and takes it for evidence that the royal power had been consolidated in David's last peaceful years, the attempt being seen not as rebellion against David but as presumption on his favour; he explains the horns of the altar as the projections to which victims were fastened, so that to grasp them claimed a sanctuary the Law denied to wilful murder, and calls Solomon's pardon extraordinary grace by Oriental measure yet cautious and conditional. Keil and Delitzsch add that the shouting carried to the fountain of Rogel, catch the assurance with a slight doubt in Jonathan's opening word, and hold that go to thy house does not banish Adonijah from court.

Henry reads the length of the dinner as evidence of security, the whole business of the anointing being finished while they sat glutting themselves, and observes that usurpers flatter themselves with hopes of success and that those are least timorous whose condition is most dangerous, so that the worthiest man brings them the worst news. He lingers on the servants' blessing, that a child on a giant's shoulders is higher than the giant, presses the irony that one who had despised Solomon as not worth inviting now dreads him as his judge, and warns that men who slight the altar in security catch at its horns too late.

Clarke sets out Jonathan's report in the four steps the messenger gave it, thinks him an observer if not a spy and confesses he cannot tell how he came by so much information so fast, says the altar was a privileged place where to molest a man was reckoned sacrilege, and reads go to thine house as excluding Adonijah from any place about the king's person or under the government.

Gill observes that many of the guests were military men, the general and his captains, who had they taken to arms would have given Solomon much trouble, and concludes that the panic was no doubt of God; he also notes that Zadok very probably applied the oil while Nathan was present approving it and declaring as a prophet that it was according to the will of God.

debates: What go to thine house means: Keil and Delitzsch hold it no banishment from court, Solomon being unwilling to open his reign with a punishment, while Clarke reads the same words as excluding Adonijah from any place about the king's person or under the government

Why the attempt collapsed so completely: Gill that the panic was of God, Ellicott that the royal power had been consolidated and the attempt was never treated as rebellion against David, Henry only that the triumphing of the wicked is short
outliers: Ellicott puzzles that of all the conspirators Adonijah alone seems to have feared punishment, his accomplices being allowed to disperse in safety and their rebellion ignored

Ellicott notes that the Law denied sanctuary to wilful murder and that it was accordingly refused to Joab afterwards, so that Adonijah, by saying King Solomon, pleads his usurpation as an act of haste
Clarke cannot tell how Jonathan came by so much information in so short a time
Gill concludes that the failure of nerve among Adonijah's military guests was no doubt of God
themes: a trumpet heard at a feast
the triumphing of the wicked is short
sanctuary claimed at the horns
a throne established by mercy
41.pericope_label: And Adonijah and all the guests that were with him heard it as they had made an end of eating. And when Joab heard the sound of the trumpet, he said, Wherefore is this noise of the city being in an uproar? And while he yet spake, behold, Jonathan the son of Abiathar the priest came: and Adonijah said unto him, Come in; for thou art a valiant man, and bringest good tidings. And Jonathan answered and said to Adonijah, Verily our lord king David hath made Solomon king. And the king hath sent with him Zadok the priest, and Nathan the prophet, and Benaiah the son of Jehoiada, and the Cherethites, and the Pelethites, and they have caused him to ride upon the king’s mule: And Zadok the priest and Nathan the prophet have anointed him king in Gihon: and they are come up from thence rejoicing, so that the city rang again. This is the noise that ye have heard. And also Solomon sitteth on the throne of the kingdom. And moreover the king’s servants came to bless our lord king David, saying, God make the name of Solomon better than thy name, and make his throne greater than thy throne. And the king bowed himself upon the bed. And also thus said the king, Blessed be the Lord God of Israel, which hath given one to sit on my throne this day, mine eyes even seeing it. And all the guests that were with Adonijah were afraid, and rose up, and went every man his way. And Adonijah feared because of Solomon, and arose, and went, and caught hold on the horns of the altar. And it was told Solomon, saying, Behold, Adonijah feareth king Solomon: for, lo, he hath caught hold on the horns of the altar, saying, Let king Solomon swear unto me to day that he will not slay his servant with the sword. And Solomon said, If he will shew himself a worthy man, there shall not an hair of him fall to the earth: but if wickedness shall be found in him, he shall die. So king Solomon sent, and they brought him down from the altar. And he came and bowed himself to king Solomon: and Solomon said unto him, Go to thine house.
